## Task T15 (narrative: work/T15/report.md)

### Arguments (6)

#### A-T15-001 — From conscious value to moral authority (position: Strongest integrated consciousness-grounding case)

- Premises: There are subjects to whom conditions can be good or bad., Assume reasons to protect subjects are objective, not merely reports of desire., Propose one necessarily good personal foundation whose relation to agents grounds binding demands.
- Bridge principles: Valence or flourishing has normative significance., Relevant others count even when helping them conflicts with my aims., The foundation is the relevant good, and its relation supplies legitimate authority., Commands are identifiable and consistent with that nature.
- Conclusion: The full account could unify welfare, reasons, obligations and accountability if every bridge is warranted; consciousness alone proves none of the later bridges.
- Claims: CL-T15-001, CL-T15-002, CL-T15-016, CL-T15-017, CL-T15-018, CL-T15-019; sources: S-T15-001
- Strongest objection: Calling a being good or creative may presuppose the normativity being explained; unity and sanctions can yield only self-interest.; strongest reply: Grounding need not be a definition or a temporal production: a defensible identity/constitution account can terminate explanation in a necessary good and a legitimate relation. This reply still owes warrant for that identity and relation.
- Depends on arguments: A-T14-004, A-T12-005
- Unresolved issues: No derivation of impartiality from mere awareness. No independent authority proof in inspected Craig transcript. No assumption that divine commands all have identical modal status.
- Review: R15 (accept)

#### A-T15-002 — Secular moral objectivity and its explanatory costs (position: Positive naturalistic account with other secular families retained)

- Premises: Human and animal conditions can affect their interests independently of current approval., A proposed moral standard considers all affected interests impartially., Correctness can diverge from present preference and social convention.
- Bridge principles: Identify the proposed natural property with normative goodness or rightness, with semantic and explanatory warrant., Justify impartiality and the treatment of conflicting interests.
- Conclusion: A physicalist ontology has a substantive route to moral realism; this route remains contested and does not settle every categorical-reason demand.
- Claims: CL-T15-003, CL-T15-004, CL-T15-005, CL-T15-016, CL-T15-019; sources: S-T15-002
- Strongest objection: A fully informed egoist may still reject impartiality; reliable preference explanation might explain moral belief while omitting moral authority.; strongest reply: Separate truth and applicability from the agent’s motivation; evaluate whether the proposed identity explains correction, practical criticism and disagreement. Other secular accounts can instead take categorical reasons or rational agency as basic, with their own costs.
- Depends on arguments: A-T14-002
- Unresolved issues: Naturalism is not a proof from evolution. Constructivism and non-natural realism reconstructed in matrix but no decisive original defender inspected. Aggregative criterion may face rights, comparability and determinate-idealization objections.
- Review: R15 (accept)

#### A-T15-003 — Suffering as evidence against specified perfect governance (position: Evidential challenge, distinct from bare logical incompatibility)

- Premises: Assume an agent knows the relevant harms and feasible alternatives, can prevent them and is perfectly good., Some suffering appears to lack a permission-justifying dependence on goods or avoidance of comparable evil.
- Bridge principles: Our inability to find such dependence is defeasible evidence of its absence in the relevant domain., A perfectly good agent does not permit harms without adequate justification; equal-value and irreplaceability qualifications must be specified.
- Conclusion: Suffering challenges that attribute package if the evidential and normative premises hold; it is not a deduction from the mere occurrence of any evil.
- Claims: CL-T15-006, CL-T15-007, CL-T15-008, CL-T15-020, CL-T15-022; sources: S-T15-003, S-T15-004
- Strongest objection: Our sample of goods, causal relations and feasible worlds may be too limited to assess what an omniscient being could justifiably permit.; strongest reply: Finite limits do not automatically erase all evidence; compare what each hypothesis actually leads us to expect and what independently supports claimed limitations. Theistic countergrounds can rationally matter.
- Depends on arguments: A-T14-005
- Unresolved issues: No measured prevalence or likelihood supplied. A hypothetical animal does not establish an actual event. Free-will and soul-making originals beyond the inspected discussions remain gaps.
- Review: R15 (accept)

#### A-T15-004 — Restoration of persons and justification of harm (position: Strong enduring-restoration reply and victim-centered challenge)

- Premises: Assume the same victims continue and receive goods capable of restoring meaningful lives., Assume their harms can be integrated without denying their reality or replacing victims with successors.
- Bridge principles: A good total life or meaningful integration can answer some questions about final loss., Antecedent permission requires a separate justification, including necessity, proportionality, rights and alternatives where applicable.
- Conclusion: Restoration can improve an account of what becomes of victims, while an account of why harms were permitted remains independently contestable.
- Claims: CL-T15-009, CL-T15-010, CL-T15-011, CL-T15-012, CL-T15-018; sources: S-T15-004, S-T15-005
- Strongest objection: A later good may quiet grief without making the original injustice permissible; one person’s reconciliation cannot speak for another victim.; strongest reply: The strongest version addresses each victim and distinguishes redemption from approval of wrongdoing; an internal consistency defense may use its own independently specified goods without claiming their actual existence is thereby proved.
- Depends on arguments: A-T13-004, A-T14-003
- Unresolved issues: The possibility and worth of divine intimacy remain contested. Identity and temporal manifestation must be specified. Adams’s later clarifications and reply to Sutherland not inspected.
- Review: R15 (accept)

#### A-T15-005 — Nonresistant nonbelief and relationship (position: Hiddenness challenge with a bounded, currently reconstructed reply)

- Premises: Assume perfect love includes being open to conscious reciprocal relationship with each capable person., Assume belief in the other’s existence is required for that specified relationship., Assume some capable persons lack belief for causes unrelated to resisting that relationship.
- Bridge principles: Perfect love entails that availability at each relevant time, rather than only eventual welfare or eventual access.
- Conclusion: If the premises hold, the specified perfectly loving personal God is excluded; other ultimate foundations remain open.
- Claims: CL-T15-013, CL-T15-014, CL-T15-015, CL-T15-021, CL-T15-023, CL-T15-024; sources: S-T15-006, S-T15-009
- Strongest objection: Howard-Snyder distinguishes a desire for relationship now from an overriding reason to enable it now. Even a well-disposed inculpable seeker might benefit from owning or refining the disposition to love. He offers defeasible prima facie reasons and epistemic caution, not proof of actual divine reasons.; strongest reply: Project comparison: a possible counterfactual disposition is not automatically resistance causing present nonbelief. Ask whether improving love can occur in an available relationship, and whether delaying access is no worse than other means once the lost relationship is counted. A defender may contest that comparison or our knowledge of it. Note18 and reply4 identify limits to this particular defense; no blanket victory is inferred.
- Depends on arguments: A-T11-004
- Unresolved issues: The1996reply addresses earlier Schellenberg; the2025argument emphasizes nonresistance causally relevant to nonbelief. Exact earlier book/reply exchange not inspected. A reason to delay developing a relationship does not automatically explain withholding the conditions of being open to one; this is the contested bridge. No observed distribution of dispositions or actual divine permission reasons. Availability, fittingness and the no-worse-alternative criterion remain disputed.
- Review: R15 (accept)

#### A-T15-006 — Goodness, authority and dependence across the package (position: Conditional synthesis and sensitivity)

- Premises: Value judgments support the moral-grounding proposal and also underwrite evil objections., Knowledge of goodness and permission-justifying reasons can have different scope., Claims of actual survival or intended moral education need evidence apart from their usefulness in a reply.
- Bridge principles: Avoid counting the same moral premise as independent evidence each time it recurs., Apply explanatory stopping-point and epistemic-access standards symmetrically to divine and secular accounts.
- Conclusion: This packet maps burdens for H-G and H-A, with conditional effects on H-I/P/S; it identifies neither a numerical posterior nor a winning full metaphysics.
- Claims: CL-T15-016, CL-T15-017, CL-T15-018, CL-T15-019, CL-T15-020, CL-T15-021, CL-T15-022; sources: —
- Strongest objection: Restricting knowledge of unknown goods need not undermine simple moral knowledge; criticism can demand unreasonable omniscience of the defender.; strongest reply: Use local rather than blanket skepticism and name what remains knowable; test whether the positive and negative inferences genuinely rely on the same inaccessible domain.
- Unresolved issues: No equal-support verdict. Removing retrospective NDE claims leaves conceptual distinctions but no new survival evidence. Rejecting moral realism changes the moral argument and some evil formulations; internal inconsistency arguments can still use an opponent’s commitments.
- Review: R15 (accept)

## Task P2T06 (narrative: work/P2T06/report.md)

### Arguments (3)

#### A-P2T06-001 — Reflective agency and the proposed authority of humanity (position: Selected Kantian constructivism)

- Premises: CL-P2T06-001, CL-P2T06-002, CL-P2T06-003, CL-P2T06-004, CL-P2T06-005
- Bridge principles: Acting reflectively requires a normative practical identity., The value of contingent identities depends on valuing humanity as their necessary source., Reasons are inherently shareable in a way that supports interpersonal demands.
- Conclusion: If these bridges hold, reflective agents owe moral obligations that do not depend merely on contingent desires.
- Claims: CL-P2T06-001, CL-P2T06-002, CL-P2T06-003, CL-P2T06-004, CL-P2T06-005, CL-P2T06-006, CL-P2T06-007, CL-P2T06-008; sources: S-P2T06-001
- Strongest objection: A need for some reason or self-conception does not yet establish an impartial moral reason; public intelligibility may leave agent-relative authority intact.; strongest reply: The proposed result is not an inference from private egoistic reasons to public ones; it challenges the assumed privacy and reconstructs principles constitutive of reflective agency.
- Unresolved issues: Necessity of normative identity for action Value of a condition versus condition of valuing Humanity-wide domain and binding publicity Concrete duty content, conflict and complete skepticism
- Review: R-P2R06 (accept)

#### A-P2T06-002 — Nagel’s direct challenge to law and identity grounding (position: Realist rival within the selected exchange)

- Premises: CL-P2T06-009, CL-P2T06-010
- Bridge principles: Reflection can reveal evaluative reasons rather than create them., A general rule can remain egoistic; regularity alone does not establish causal agency.
- Conclusion: The constructive account needs an additional justification of its law-like and interpersonal requirements, and may reverse the direction of normative explanation.
- Claims: CL-P2T06-009, CL-P2T06-010, CL-P2T06-011, CL-P2T06-012; sources: S-P2T06-002, S-P2T06-003
- Strongest objection: Treating reflection as an already impersonal standpoint may assume the generality it seeks to justify; locating reasons in a standpoint does not alone settle whether they are discovered or constructed.; strongest reply: Evaluate the actual reasons for treating persons’ interests as significant; moral concern need not be replaced by a self-image or payoff.
- Unresolved issues: Independent warrant for the evaluative judgment Status of the reflective standpoint No comprehensive non-natural realism assessment
- Review: R-P2R06 (accept)

#### A-P2T06-003 — The constitutive reply and its explicit scope (position: Korsgaard’s actual response to Nagel)

- Premises: CL-P2T06-011, CL-P2T06-012, CL-P2T06-013
- Bridge principles: Distinguishing willing from a succession of impulses requires commitments across relevantly similar possible occasions., Endorsing a reason from a practical identity need not replace its other-directed content., The rules of reflection constrain endorsement rather than making any choice correct.
- Conclusion: The reply offers formal universality and a response to reward-based interpretations; its full moral conclusion still depends on humanity and publicity arguments.
- Claims: CL-P2T06-003, CL-P2T06-004, CL-P2T06-005, CL-P2T06-010, CL-P2T06-011, CL-P2T06-012, CL-P2T06-013, CL-P2T06-014; sources: S-P2T06-003, S-P2T06-001, S-P2T06-002
- Strongest objection: Constitutive agency rules need independent defense; even granted general commitments, the all-persons domain and binding force of another’s reasons remain open.; strongest reply: A rule internal to an activity need not be an arbitrary external command; the theory distinguishes genuine choice from impulse while retaining the content of concern for others.
- Depends on arguments: A-P2T06-001, A-P2T06-002
- Unresolved issues: Formal universality is not full moral universalism Fully reflective endorsement and partial nonmoral obligations Complete skepticism expressly left open
- Review: R-P2R06 (accept)

## Task P2T07 (narrative: work/P2T07/report.md)

### Arguments (5)

#### A-P2T07-001 — Enoch’s indispensability strategy: introduction, partial book text and direct author reply (position: For justified belief in irreducible normative truth)

- Premises: Deliberation is rationally non-optional., Normative truths and belief in them are instrumentally indispensable to that project.
- Bridge principles: Indispensability to an appropriate non-optional project can justify ontological commitment; explanatory indispensability is a related instance.
- Conclusion: There is reason to believe irreducibly normative truths exist; a further moral bridge is needed.
- Claims: CL-P2T07-003, CL-P2T07-004, CL-P2T07-010, CL-P2T07-014, CL-P2T07-019, CL-P2T07-020; sources: S-P2T07-001, S-P2T07-003
- Strongest objection: Lenman's thin/thick dilemma challenges joint satisfaction of both premises.; strongest reply: Enoch distinguishes merited standards, first-person warrant and value-sensitive instrumental indispensability.
- Unresolved issues: Developed chapter3 pp.53–83, including epistemological defense, remain uninspected. Chapter4 moral bridge and§5.1 now read; both are qualified and do not establish the missing derivation or premise truth. Rejection of alternatives remains incomplete, explicitly at p.84 and§5.1.
- Review: R-P2R07 (accept)

#### A-P2T07-002 — Lenman's schmeliberation countercase (position: Against joint indispensability premises)

- Premises: Thin practical reflection uses scrutinized contingent concerns., This activity admits success/error and deliberation-like phenomenology without robust truth., Thickening it threatens non-optionality.
- Bridge principles: A sufficient alternative defeats indispensability.
- Conclusion: Robust truths have not been shown indispensable to unavoidable deliberation.
- Claims: CL-P2T07-005, CL-P2T07-006; sources: S-P2T07-002
- Strongest objection: Standards and similarity may not supply the deserved allegiance claimed necessary.; strongest reply: Lenman regards stable concerns and critical reflection as sufficient without further ratification of the whole.
- Unresolved issues: Sufficiency of the thin project disputed. Not every Humean or epistemic-normativity response inspected. No empirical generalization from phenomenology.
- Review: R-P2R07 (accept)

#### A-P2T07-003 — Enoch's direct reply to schmeliberation (position: Defends remaining justificatory force)

- Premises: Choosing versus picking is not proved exhaustive., Formal standards may lack merited allegiance., Replacement may preserve behavior while diminishing project value., Justificatory evidence can vary without relativizing truth.
- Bridge principles: A weaker replacement need not defeat the specified instrumental indispensability., Phenomenology supplies claimed warrant, not truth-making.
- Conclusion: Lenman's alternative does not by itself remove Enoch's claimed reason to believe.
- Claims: CL-P2T07-008, CL-P2T07-009, CL-P2T07-010; sources: S-P2T07-003
- Strongest objection: Deserved allegiance may restate the disputed demand; private commitment needs a truth-directed epistemic bridge.; strongest reply: Enoch invokes broader indispensability epistemology, permits premise error and distinguishes diminished projects from identical behavior.
- Depends on arguments: A-P2T07-001
- Unresolved issues: Developed chapter3 vindication on pp.53–83 remains absent; opening and final p.84 are now read. Expressivism response expressly preliminary at862. Moorean criterion unsupplied863–864. Color-blindness analogy is not validation.
- Review: R-P2R07 (accept)

#### A-P2T07-004 — Enoch’s conditional moral bridge (position: For extending justified general normative realism to robust moral realism, given moral objectivity)

- Premises: Assume chapter 2 has established moral objectivity., Assume chapter3 has supplied justified robust general normative realism, after objections have been considered., Common objections concern normativity generally; moral facts are proposed to be of the same relevant ontological kind., The chapter 4 response argues for a non-wholly-contingent connection between morality and reasons, explicitly limited to a weak claim.
- Bridge principles: A disjunctive treatment of moral and other normative facts needs a rationale once shared objections and the proposed categorical-reason concern lose their force., This is a defeasible motivation challenge, not entailment from the two antecedent conclusions.
- Conclusion: On those assumptions, familiar alternatives to robust moral realism are under-motivated; other unconsidered motivations remain possible.
- Claims: CL-P2T07-003, CL-P2T07-015, CL-P2T07-016, CL-P2T07-017; sources: S-P2T07-001
- Strongest objection: Shared objections can impose continuing costs, moral and other normativity may differ in relevant respects, and the antecedent chapter3 case has not been fully checked. Naturalist or expressivist alternatives may have further motivations.; strongest reply: Enoch contrasts accumulating costs with an objection defeated at the level of kind, and argues that moral objectivity requires normative privilege rather than mere etiquette. He expressly limits the result to a weak moral-reason link and an open-ended challenge.
- Depends on arguments: A-P2T07-001
- Unresolved issues: Antecedent objectivity and indispensability arguments not certified by this chapter’s reading No guarantee of a reason in every case or overriding moral priority Possible further rationale for a mixed or naturalist view; §5.1 remains open to successful reduction
- Review: R-P2R07 (accept)

#### A-P2T07-005 — Enoch’s qualified resistance to naturalist reduction (position: Defeasible initial suspicion of reduction with openness to successful detailed proposals)

- Premises: From the deliberative standpoint, Enoch finds purely natural descriptions insufficient without normative background commitments., Conceptual differences alone do not settle property identities, and a naturalist can claim the proposed base is itself normative., Familiar a priori/a posteriori objections and the response to Schroeder are not a conclusive general irreducibility proof.
- Bridge principles: An initial intuition can bear defeasible weight without being unrevisable., Specific reductions must be assessed by their details and theoretical virtues; inability to refute one is not itself metaphysical evidence for it.
- Conclusion: Enoch retains suspicion but allows a strong specific, including token-level, reduction to overturn the initial commitment.
- Claims: CL-P2T07-018, CL-P2T07-019, CL-P2T07-020; sources: S-P2T07-001
- Strongest objection: The initial normative-force intuition may encode the disputed non-naturalism; the naturalist may accept concept difference while denying metaphysical difference.; strongest reply: Enoch acknowledges this impasse and treats it as a limit on the argument, not a victory; he asks for detailed reductions capable of earning their theoretical costs and explicitly permits revising his intuition.
- Depends on arguments: A-P2T07-001
- Unresolved issues: No separately inspected Schroeder original or full naturalism critic/reply chain No supplied successful token-level theory; no refutation of all reductions How the incomplete chapter3 indispensability case survives a reduction that preserves deliberation remains contested
- Review: R-P2R07 (accept)
